title: How Target Knows What You Want Before You Do
coreMove: Read the habit trail from the outside, then test whether using it serves the person or quietly steers them.
sourcePressure: Target's buying patterns show that routines become commercially readable data. The chapter is about partial prediction, life-stage inference, familiar placement, and the ethical line between helpful personalization and manipulation.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version turns this into generic privacy panic, omniscient AI prediction, or marketing tips. The writer must keep the mechanism narrower: repeated actions leave trails, and familiar placement can lower resistance to novelty.

hook: A creepy company knows everything about you.
An AI predicts your whole life.
counterintuition: Most people think data is private, but actually companies know everything.
Ignoring whether the personalization helps or manipulates.
tryThisNow: Set a timer for ninety seconds and delete an app.
Collect more customer data with no ethical test.

exampleSpecs.domain: regional grocer detecting a low-sodium cooking shift
exampleSpecs.audience: a loyalty-program manager deciding what to do with a sudden pattern in regular basket data
exampleSpecs.stakes: a helpful nudge could support a health change, while a blunt coupon could expose something private at the checkout
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The manager circles low-sodium broth, unsalted crackers, and the same Tuesday pickup slot, then chooses a familiar receipt placement for general heart-healthy staples instead of a message that announces a diagnosis.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A receipt shows low-sodium broth beside the same Tuesday pickup slot.
mustAvoid: privacy panic with no design choice

exampleSpecs.domain: hardware store project purchases revealing a first winter in a new house
exampleSpecs.audience: a merchandising analyst deciding how to place unfamiliar maintenance products
exampleSpecs.stakes: new homeowners need help, but a store can turn uncertainty into overselling
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The analyst predicts the shopper will resist a big winterization banner, then places pipe insulation beside the paint trays and furnace filters already in the basket so novelty rides with familiar projects.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A cart holds paint trays, furnace filters, and one roll of pipe insulation.

exampleSpecs.domain: music streaming app reading late-night replay patterns
exampleSpecs.audience: a product lead reviewing whether to personalize after repeated 2 a.m. listening sessions
exampleSpecs.stakes: the same inference could help a listener wind down or push them deeper into sleepless autoplay
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The lead points to the 2 a.m. replay cluster and asks whether the next card should be a sleep-timer shortcut or another endless mix, making the ethical line visible in the interface choice.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A replay graph spikes at 2 a.m. beside a glowing sleep-timer button.

exampleSpecs.domain: checking-account transaction pattern before recurring overdrafts
exampleSpecs.audience: a bank service designer deciding between a warning, a fee product, and silence
exampleSpecs.stakes: predictive inference can prevent avoidable fees or quietly monetize a customer's tightest week
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After a complaint, the designer lays payroll dates, grocery debits, and overdraft fees on one timeline and sees that the trail was readable before the fee; the next design choice must pass a help-versus-steer test.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A transaction timeline shows payroll, grocery debits, and overdraft fees.

exampleSpecs.domain: running-shoe retailer using purchase cadence and blister-pad add-ons
exampleSpecs.audience: a store analyst who wants to personalize without making customers feel watched
exampleSpecs.stakes: the data can prevent injury through a fitting check or exploit anxiety with unnecessary gear
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the change, the email screams injury risk; after revision, the blister-pad add-on and worn-shoe timing trigger a normal fitting invitation tucked beside the usual reorder reminder.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A worn-shoe photo sits beside a blister-pad receipt.

exampleSpecs.domain: meal-kit service noticing a shift from shared dinners to single-serving orders
exampleSpecs.audience: a retention manager deciding whether to chase a churn risk or respect a life change
exampleSpecs.stakes: a company can make a hard transition easier or turn a private change into relentless pressure to buy
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The manager sees family-size dinners give way to single-serving soups and skipped Fridays, then chooses a pause-and-adjust card in the normal menu flow rather than a barrage of win-back discounts.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Single-serving soup cards replace family-size dinners in a menu queue.

skillTargets: infer what a repeated external data trail can and cannot reveal
distinguish partial prediction from omniscient surveillance claims
choose personalization that uses familiar placement without exposing or manipulating the person
evaluate whether a commercial use of habit data serves the user's interest or exploits their vulnerability

tryThisNowSpec: Look at one repeated trail you leave outside yourself, such as purchases, logins, routes, or skips. Write what it might reveal, then draw a line between a helpful use and a manipulative one.
